idiom_name: sealed interface Either<L, R> + Left/Right records + pattern switch
implementation_notes: Java has no Either in the JDK, so it is written as a sealed interface with exactly two record implementations: the compiler then knows the hierarchy is closed, and a pattern switch over it is checked for exhaustiveness (Java 21), which turns 'handle both cases' into a compile-time property instead of a convention. On Java 17 the same records work with an instanceof pattern chain, and before that - or when the combinators are wanted for free - Vavr's Either<L,R> is the established library. The convention is right-biased: Right carries the value and Left the reason.
pitfalls: Sealing restricts only direct subclasses: declare a permitted subtype non-sealed and the exhaustiveness guarantee disappears, so the compiler starts demanding a default arm.
Generics are invariant, so Either<String, Integer> is not an Either<Object, Object>: utility methods need their own type parameters instead of widening casts.
Records are final and value-equal, but their components are shallowly immutable - a mutable reason object inside Left still changes and breaks hashCode/equals in collections.
Vavr's Either is right-biased, so map/flatMap leave a Left untouched and transforming the reason needs mapLeft; conversions through Optional or Future drop the reason entirely.

variants.name: Sealed interface with instanceof pattern chain
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface Either<L, R> + records + instanceof chain
variants.implementation_notes: With Java 17 the sealed interface and its records are available but pattern switches are not, so the eliminator is an instanceof pattern chain ending in a defensive throw: the compiler cannot prove the chain total, and that trailing throw is the only thing standing between a newly added case and a silent fall-through. The type's shape is identical to the Java 21 realization, so raising the floor later is a local change in the consumer.
pitfalls: Without pattern switch the compiler cannot see the chain as exhaustive, so forgetting the trailing throw turns an unhandled case into a silent null return.
Generic instanceof patterns need the type arguments spelled out (Left<String, Integer>); a raw pattern binds an unchecked value and the reason access loses type safety.

variants.name: Vavr Either<L, R>
variants.implementation_notes: Vavr is a functional library for Java 8+ that documents Either<L, R> as a right-biased interface whose Left holds the failure and Right the value, with map/flatMap/filter/fold, safe extraction through getOrElse/orElse and conversions such as toTry, toValidation and toOption. Choose it when the toolchain cannot move past Java 8, when the codebase already uses Vavr's persistent collections and Try, or when the combinators should not be written by hand; the cost is a dependency and a second Either type in the project.
pitfalls: get() throws on a Left and is the Vavr unwrap: the safe exits are getOrElse/getOrElseGet/orElse, with toTry() as the bridge back into exception-based code.
The left/right projections are deprecated because the type is right-biased - using left()/right() in new code means carrying deprecated API into the codebase.
toValidation() switches from short-circuiting to accumulating failures; that changes the semantics of a chain, so the conversion has to be a deliberate choice.
